My grandmother made it in a dented pot that had seen decades of Sunday lunches, never once measuring the vinegar or soy sauce. She cooked by smell and by memory, tasting as she went, and somehow it came out the same every time.

The beauty of adobo is its simplicity. Chicken, vinegar, soy sauce, garlic, bay leaves, and black peppercorns simmer together until the meat turns tender and the sauce becomes rich, tangy, and deeply savory. The kitchen fills with a sharp, garlicky aroma that pulls everyone toward the table long before the rice is ready.

Sunlight looks white, but it's actually all the colors of the rainbow mixed together. You can see this when light passes through a prism, or when raindrops split it into a rainbow.

Light travels in waves, and each color has a different wavelength. Red light has long, stretched-out waves. Blue light has short, choppy ones.

When sunlight enters Earth's atmosphere, it crashes into tiny gas molecules, mostly nitrogen and oxygen. These molecules are much smaller than the light waves themselves, and they scatter short waves far more strongly than long ones. So red and orange light mostly zoom straight through, while blue light gets bounced around in every direction, like a pinball. This is called Rayleigh scattering.

Because blue light is bouncing all over the sky, it reaches your eyes from every direction. That's why the whole sky glows blue.

Violet light scatters even more than blue, so why isn't the sky purple? The sun gives off less violet, and our eyes aren't very sensitive to it.

Sunsets work the same way. When the sun is low, its light travels through much more air to reach you. Most of the blue gets scattered away, leaving the reds and oranges.

When you visit a website, your browser downloads many files: images, fonts, stylesheets, and scripts. Downloading takes time, so your browser saves copies of these files on your device. This storage area is called the **cache**.

The next time you visit that site, your browser checks its cache first. If it already has a file, it loads the saved copy instead of downloading it again. That's why a website often loads faster on your second visit.

It's a bit like keeping groceries in your kitchen. Instead of going to the store every time you want milk, you grab it from the fridge.

But what if the website changes? Like milk, cached files have an expiration date. Websites tell your browser how long each file can be kept. Once that time is up, the browser asks the website, "Has this changed?" If not, it keeps using its copy. If so, it downloads the new version.

Occasionally the cache causes problems, such as showing an outdated version of a page. That's why tech support often suggests "clearing your cache," which deletes the saved files and forces your browser to download everything fresh.

In short, the cache trades a little storage space for faster browsing and less data use.

The phone had been ringing for eleven minutes before Marit admitted it wasn't the wind.

She stood on the gallery with her tea going cold, watching the tide drag itself off the skerries below. Thirty-one years she had kept the light at Hallow Point, and the sea had delivered her plenty: a crate of Portuguese oranges, a prosthetic leg, once a piano lid with the hinges still bright. Never anything that asked for her attention so insistently.

She took the stairs, one hundred and forty-two of them, her knees counting each. Outside, the rocks were slick with bladderwrack and the morning was the colour of old pewter. The sound led her past the boat slip to a shelf of basalt the gulls favoured.

It lay wedged in a crevice above the waterline. Not one of the flat glass ones the supply-boat lads carried, but a telephone: black Bakelite, rotary dial, heavy as a brick. Its cord trailed six feet across the stone and ended in frayed copper, connected to nothing.

It rang again. The receiver trembled in its cradle.

Marit wiped her palms on her cardigan and lifted it to her ear.

"Finally," said her own voice. "You don't have long."

The phone was ringing when Tobias Wren came down to check the mooring lines, and at first he took it for a gull.

He had kept the light at Carrow Point for nineteen years, and in that time the sea had delivered him many things: a crate of Portuguese oranges, a child's red boot, half a piano. It had never delivered anything that asked for his attention so insistently.

He found it wedged in a cleft between two slabs of basalt, just above the tide line. It was an old rotary telephone, black and heavy, its cord trailing into the kelp and ending in frayed copper. There was no wire running to shore. There was no wire running anywhere.

It rang again. The sound was bright and domestic, absurd against the grind of the swell.

Tobias looked back at the lighthouse, then out at the gray water, as though someone might be watching for his reaction. Nobody was. Nobody had been for a long time.

He crouched, knees complaining, and wiped the salt from the receiver with his sleeve. The bakelite was warm. That troubled him more than the ringing did.

On the seventh ring, he picked it up.

# *Frankenstein* by Mary Shelley (1818)

**Plot:** Victor Frankenstein, a brilliant and ambitious young scientist, becomes obsessed with discovering the secret of life. After months of feverish work, he animates a creature assembled from corpses, then flees in horror at what he has made. Abandoned, the Creature teaches himself language and longs for human connection, but his appearance earns him only fear and violence. Embittered, he murders Victor's young brother and demands that Victor build him a female companion. Victor begins, then destroys the unfinished mate, and the Creature retaliates by killing Victor's closest friend and his bride, Elizabeth. Victor pursues him into the Arctic, where he dies aboard an explorer's ship. The Creature, grieving over his creator's body, vanishes into the ice to end his own life.

**Themes:** Shelley's novel warns against unchecked ambition, showing how the pursuit of knowledge without foresight can bring ruin. It is equally a story about responsibility: Victor's true failure is not creating life but abandoning it. The Creature's transformation from gentle to vengeful raises the question of whether monsters are born or made by rejection and isolation. Throughout, the novel blurs the line between creator and creation, asking which of the two is truly monstrous.

**Frankenstein by Mary Shelley (1818)**

**Plot:** Victor Frankenstein, a brilliant young scientist from Geneva, becomes obsessed with uncovering the secret of life. After years of feverish study, he assembles a creature from dead body parts and brings it to life. Horrified by what he has made, he abandons it. The creature, intelligent and sensitive, wanders alone and learns language by secretly observing a family. Rejected by everyone he meets because of his appearance, he grows bitter and seeks out his creator. When Victor refuses to build him a companion, the creature takes revenge by killing those Victor loves, including his friend Henry and his bride Elizabeth. Victor pursues him into the Arctic, where he dies aboard an explorer's ship. The creature mourns him and vanishes into the ice, intending to end his own life.

**Themes:** The novel explores the dangers of unchecked ambition and the pursuit of knowledge without regard for consequences. It also asks what creators owe to what they create, since Victor's neglect, more than the creature's nature, drives the tragedy. Isolation runs throughout: both Victor and the creature suffer from loneliness, suggesting that cruelty is often born from rejection. Finally, Shelley questions who the real monster is, blurring the line between human and inhuman.

Starting today, every edit you make offline is saved to your device and synced automatically the moment you reconnect. Write on a flight, revise a draft in the subway, or capture ideas at a remote cabin. When you are back online, your changes appear across all your devices without any extra steps.

**What's new**

* **Automatic sync:** Offline edits upload in the background as soon as a connection returns.
* **Smart merging:** If you edited the same note on two devices, we combine the changes line by line. When edits truly conflict, both versions are kept so nothing is lost.
* **Sync status indicator:** A small icon in the corner of each note shows whether it is saved locally, syncing, or fully up to date.
* **Full offline access:** Create, edit, organize, and search all of your notes without a signal.

**How to get it**

Update to version 4.2 on iOS, Android, Mac, or Windows. Offline sync is turned on by default, so there is nothing to configure.

We built this because you asked for it, and we are grateful for the feedback.

Happy writing!

I ducked into a tiny café in North Beach, where the windows steamed up and the espresso was strong enough to revive me. From there, I wandered through City Lights Bookstore, losing an hour among creaky wooden floors and shelves of Beat poetry while the storm drummed overhead. By afternoon, the cable cars rattled past with their bells clanging, slick tracks gleaming under the gray sky. I warmed up at the Ferry Building with a sourdough bowl of clam chowder, watching ferries push across the choppy bay. The hills, usually a workout, turned into shimmering streams reflecting neon signs and taillights. Rain may not be on every traveler's wish list, but it showed me a quieter, cozier side of the city. Sometimes the best travel days are the ones you never planned for.

**Great Broth, Long Wait**

The tonkotsu broth here is the real thing: creamy, deeply porky, and rich without being greasy. You can taste the hours of simmering in every spoonful. The noodles had a nice springy chew, the chashu was tender, and the soft-boiled egg had that perfect jammy center.

Getting to that bowl, though, tested my patience. We waited ten minutes to be greeted, another fifteen to order, and nearly forty for our food on a Tuesday night with half the tables empty. Our server was friendly but clearly stretched thin, and no one checked on us or refilled water until we flagged someone down.

Is it worth it? Yes, with caveats. Come when you're not in a hurry, and maybe have a snack beforehand. If they sort out the staffing, this could easily be the best ramen in the neighborhood. For now, it's four stars for the food, two for the service.

Remote work, as most companies practice it, hurts junior engineers more than it helps them. The early years of an engineering career are an apprenticeship, and apprenticeship runs on proximity: overhearing a senior colleague debug a production issue, watching how a design disagreement gets resolved, asking a "dumb" question in passing without the formality of scheduling a call. Remote setups strip away that ambient learning. A junior who is stuck may spin for hours rather than interrupt someone over Slack, and feedback shrinks to terse code review comments that explain what to change but rarely why. Seniors, who already have their skills and networks, enjoy the flexibility while juniors quietly pay the cost in slower growth and weaker relationships with the people who will later vouch for them. That said, the damage is not inevitable. Teams that pair program deliberately, write down their reasoning, and treat mentorship as real work can close much of the gap, and remote hiring opens doors for talented people far from tech hubs. But those teams are the exception. Absent that investment, a new engineer learns far faster sitting near more experienced ones, and companies that pretend otherwise are borrowing against their own future talent.

Remote work, in my view, hurts junior engineers more than it helps them, at least when companies treat it as a simple change of location. Early career growth depends on absorbing things nobody thinks to write down: how a senior colleague debugs a stubborn problem, how tradeoffs get argued in a hallway, when to push back on a vague requirement. In an office, that knowledge leaks out constantly and for free. At home, a junior engineer has to ask for it, and asking carries a cost. Every question becomes a deliberate message that might interrupt someone, so many newcomers stay stuck for hours rather than risk looking incompetent. The result is slower learning, weaker relationships, and less visibility when promotions are decided. That said, the damage is not inevitable. Teams that pair program regularly, hold open office hours, document decisions, and assign dedicated mentors can close much of the gap, and remote roles do open doors for talented people who live far from expensive tech hubs. But those practices require real effort, and most organizations do not invest in them. Until they do, a junior engineer choosing between two equal offers should favor the one with experienced teammates sitting nearby.

Running and swimming are both excellent cardiovascular workouts, but they suit different bodies and goals.

Running is the more accessible option. You need only a pair of shoes and a stretch of road, and you can start the moment you step outside. It burns calories quickly, strengthens the legs and core, and, because it is weight-bearing, helps build bone density. The trade-off is impact: each stride sends force through the ankles, knees, and hips, which makes overuse injuries like shin splints and runner's knee common, especially for beginners who ramp up too fast.

Swimming is gentler. Water supports your body weight, so joints are spared while nearly every major muscle group works against resistance. This makes it ideal for people with arthritis, injuries, or extra weight, and it builds upper-body strength that running largely neglects. However, it requires pool access and reasonable technique; poor form limits how hard you can work. It also does little for bone strength.

For calorie burn, the two are comparable at similar intensities, though running usually edges ahead per minute.

Ultimately, the best choice is the one you'll do consistently. Many people combine them, using swimming for recovery and full-body conditioning and running for convenience and bone health.

Swimming is much gentler on the joints. Water supports your body, which makes it a good choice for people with injuries, arthritis, or extra weight. It also works the whole body, engaging the shoulders, back, core, and legs in a single session. However, it requires access to a pool or open water, and good technique takes time to learn. Without it, workouts can feel frustrating and less effective. Swimming also does little for bone density.

In terms of calories burned, the two are roughly comparable at similar effort levels, though running usually has a slight edge.

The best choice depends on your goals, your joints, and what you enjoy. Many people combine both, using swimming for recovery and running for intensity.

**1/** Clever code impresses for the ten minutes it takes to write. Simple code pays off for the ten years it takes to maintain. Here's why boring wins.

**2/** Code is read far more often than it's written. That one-liner with nested ternaries saved you four lines once. It costs every future reader five minutes, forever.

**3/** Kernighan's law: debugging is twice as hard as writing the code in the first place. So if you write the cleverest code you're capable of, you are by definition not smart enough to debug it.

**4/** Requirements change. Simple code is easy to modify and easy to delete. Clever abstractions bake in guesses about the future, and when those guesses turn out wrong, you have to untangle the cleverness before you can fix anything.

**5/** Simple isn't easy, though. Finding the plain solution often takes more thought than the tricky one. When you do need a trick, like in a hot loop, isolate it and comment why. Spend your cleverness on the problem, not the syntax.

**1/5**
Clever code feels great to write. Simple code feels great to read. Code gets read far more often than it gets written, so guess which one pays off. Here's why boring wins. 🧵

**2/5**
Debugging is harder than writing. Kernighan said it best: if you write code as cleverly as you possibly can, you are by definition not smart enough to debug it. Leave yourself some headroom.

**3/5**
Your code has an audience: the teammate who joined last week, the on-call engineer at 3am, and you in six months with zero memory of what you were thinking. None of them want a puzzle. They want to understand it fast and move on.

**4/5**
Simple code is cheap to change. Requirements shift, and when they do, plain logic bends while clever tricks break. That elegant one liner packed with assumptions becomes a full rewrite the moment one assumption stops being true.

**5/5**
Clever code shows off the author. Simple code serves the reader. The real skill is taking a hard problem and making the solution look obvious. Write code that makes people say "oh, that's it?" That's the compliment to aim for.
